triage.name: Cellulitis
triage.reason: Acute spreading skin infection with fever and erythema; diagnosis is clinical and mimics DVT and necrotizing infection, a strong teaching case.

demographics: More common in adults than children
Slightly more common in men in many series
More common in people with lower socioeconomic status and in those with repeated healthcare contact

risk_factors.text: Break in the skin such as a cut, scrape, insect bite, or surgical wound
Tinea pedis with fissures between the toes
Chronic leg swelling or venous insufficiency
Lymphedema or prior lymph node removal
Prior episode of cellulitis at the same site
Water exposure or swimming in fresh water with an open wound

social_history: Occupations with skin trauma such as farming or construction
exposures: Fresh water exposure with an open wound

chief_complaints.text: My leg is red, swollen, and hurts
My arm is red and tender

hpi.onset: Fairly rapid, over 1–3 days; often the patient can point to a bite, scrape, or crack in the skin that came first
hpi.progression: The area of redness and swelling enlarges steadily; pain and warmth increase; fever and chills may develop as it spreads
hpi.location: Most often the lower leg, but can be the arm, face, or any site of skin breakdown
hpi.radiation: No radiation; the process spreads locally rather than following a nerve
hpi.quality: Burning, throbbing, and tender to the touch; the skin feels tight and hot
hpi.severity: Moderate; pain is often 4–7/10 and worse with standing or walking
aggravating: Standing or walking on the affected leg

associated_symptoms.text: Swollen or tender lymph nodes near the area
A red streak running up the limb
Clear or pus-filled drainage from the wound

pertinent_negatives: Pain out of proportion to the exam or rapidly worsening pain
Skin turning dusky, gray, or black
Crepitus or crackling under the skin
Numbness or loss of sensation in the area
Severe pain with light touch out of keeping with the redness
Recent long flight or immobility with calf pain
Joint swelling with inability to bear weight
Recurrent boils or draining sinus tracts

positives.text: Red, warm, swollen area of skin
A break in the skin, bite, or scrape at the edge of the redness
Blisters or peeling skin over the red area
Drainage or pus from the wound

negatives: Skin cracking or popping when pressed
Rash on both legs in the same pattern

positives.text: Pain with movement of the nearby joint

negatives: Joint locked or unable to bear weight
Muscle weakness out of proportion to pain

positives.text: Tender lymph nodes near the area

negatives: Numbness or tingling in the affected limb
Severe pain out of proportion to exam

atypical.how_it_differs: May have little or no fever and less pain; redness can be mistaken for chronic venous changes, and they can become confused or hypotensive quickly.
Often presents with a foot ulcer or a deeper, less obvious infection; neuropathy can blunt pain and the redness may be less striking.
Can progress faster and with fewer local signs; fever may be the main clue and unusual organisms are more likely.
Often follows an insect bite or minor trauma; the child may refuse to walk or use the limb and may be fussy rather than describing pain.
Presents with irritability, poor feeding, and fever; the skin finding may be subtle or on the diaper area.
Lower leg swelling is common in pregnancy, so cellulitis can be mistaken for normal swelling; redness and warmth help distinguish it.
Skin folds and leg swelling make the redness harder to see and the area harder to examine; recurrent episodes are more common.
missing_classic_features: Easy visualization of the affected area

atypical.how_it_differs: Fluid overload and chronic skin changes can mask or mimic cellulitis; antibiotic dosing needs adjustment.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable at rest, no distress
general.moderate: Mildly ill-appearing, favors the affected limb, uncomfortable with movement
general.severe: Ill-appearing, flushed, tachycardic, reluctant to move the limb
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale or mottled, diaphoretic, may be confused or lethargic

findings.maneuver: Palpate the red area and compare with the unaffected side
findings.finding: Increased warmth of the involved skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the limb for swelling, comparing sides
findings.finding: Localized swelling or pitting edema of the affected limb

findings.maneuver: Search the skin at and around the edge of the redness for a wound, bite, or fissure
findings.finding: A break in the skin, insect bite, scrape, or interdigital fissure

Inspect the surface of the red area

Serous or purulent drainage from the wound

findings.finding: No fluctuant mass or drainable pocket

findings.maneuver: Palpate the skin and subcutaneous tissue for crackling
Inspect the skin color and check for sloughing or anesthesia

No symmetric bilateral rash with weeping or stasis changes

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not rule out cellulitis; mild cases often have normal labs.
Nonspecific; helps track response but does not distinguish cellulitis from a deep infection.
Elevated lactate with hypotension or organ dysfunction suggests sepsis and need for IV antibiotics and fluids.
Rises with dehydration or sepsis; guides antibiotic dosing.
From poor intake, fever, and third-spacing.
Uncontrolled hyperglycemia in diabetes predisposes to and worsens skin infection.
Marked elevation with pain out of proportion should raise concern for necrotizing infection or myositis.
May help gauge bacterial burden and sepsis risk but is not required for diagnosis.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before antibiotics or imaging that could affect a pregnancy.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected abscess or fluid collection beneath the cellulitis

findings.text: Diffuse subcutaneous thickening and increased echogenicity (edema)
Well-defined fluid collection with posterior acoustic enhancement (abscess)

imaging.study: CT of the affected area with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Concern for deep infection, necrotizing fasciitis, or abscess not seen on ultrasound

Asymmetric fascial thickening with fluid tracking along fascia
No gas or fascial involvement (argues against necrotizing infection)

imaging.study: MRI of the affected area with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Equivocal deep infection or when CT is unavailable or contraindicated

findings.text: Fascial enhancement and fluid along fascial planes
Muscle involvement with T2 hyperintensity and enhancement

imaging.study: Plain radiograph of the affected limb

initial.why: Looks for leukocytosis and left shift; normal does not exclude cellulitis
Assesses hydration, renal function, and glucose before antibiotic dosing
Supports bacterial infection and helps track response
initial.only_if: moderate or severe disease or diagnostic uncertainty

initial.why: Screens for sepsis when fever, tachycardia, or hypotension is present
initial.only_if: systemic signs or concern for sepsis

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before antibiotics or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

initial.test: Ultrasound of the affected soft tissue
initial.why: Distinguishes abscess from simple cellulitis when a fluid collection is suspected
initial.only_if: fluctuance, severe pain, or failure to improve

supporting.why: May support bacterial infection and sepsis risk when the diagnosis is unclear
Evaluates for muscle involvement when pain is out of proportion to findings
supporting.only_if: severe pain or suspected necrotizing infection

supporting.test: CT of the affected area with IV contrast
supporting.why: Defines deep infection or abscess when ultrasound is nondiagnostic
supporting.only_if: suspected deep infection, abscess, or necrotizing fasciitis

supporting.test: MRI of the affected area with and without contrast
supporting.why: Clarifies deep infection when CT is equivocal or contraindicated

not_indicated.why: No role in diagnosing cellulitis; may be considered only if DVT is a competing diagnosis
Not needed unless the patient is on anticoagulants or has bleeding
Not needed unless the patient is on anticoagulants or has bleeding
Not indicated unless urinary symptoms or sepsis of unclear source

not_indicated.test: Plain radiograph of the affected limb
not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management of uncomplicated cellulitis

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical; do not delay antibiotics for cultures or imaging in uncomplicated cases
Pregnancy test before antibiotics or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Look for an abscess when there is fluctuance or failure to improve; ultrasound or CT if uncertain
Suspect necrotizing infection with pain out of proportion, dusky skin, bullae, crepitus, or rapid progression; urgent surgical consultation and CT if needed
Blood cultures are low yield in mild cellulitis and are reserved for severe disease, immunocompromised patients, or unusual exposures

differential.name: Deep vein thrombosis
differential.why_considered: Unilateral leg swelling, pain, and warmth are the classic shared presentation with lower extremity cellulitis.
differential.trigger: Unilateral leg swelling with calf pain but no clear skin break, no spreading erythema, and no fever

history: Recent long travel, immobilization, surgery, or active cancer
Prior DVT or known thrombophilia
Calf pain and swelling that came on gradually without a wound or bite
No fever or chills
exam: Calf tenderness and asymmetric calf circumference without a sharply warm, red, spreading plaque
No skin break, fissure, or bite at the edge of the swelling
No lymphangitic streaking
labs: D-dimer negative makes DVT unlikely in low-risk patients
imaging: Compression ultrasound of the leg shows a non-compressible vein with intraluminal thrombus
Soft tissue ultrasound shows no subcutaneous thickening or hyperemia

differential.name: Necrotizing soft tissue infection
differential.why_considered: Begins as a red, painful, swollen area that can be mistaken for simple cellulitis early in its course.
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to the exam, dusky or gray skin, bullae with sloughing, crepitus, or rapid progression over hours

history: Pain far worse than the visible redness suggests
Rapid worsening over hours rather than days
Diabetes, immunosuppression, injection drug use, or recent surgery
Systemic toxicity with high fever and feeling very unwell
exam: Dusky, gray, or black skin; bullae with sloughing
Crepitus or crackling under the skin
Sensory loss or anesthesia over the involved area
Severe pain with light touch or passive movement
Tachycardia and hypotension out of keeping with the local findings
labs: Markedly elevated WBC, CRP, and lactate
Hyponatremia and renal dysfunction in advanced disease
imaging: CT shows asymmetric fascial thickening, fluid tracking along fascia, and subcutaneous or intramuscular gas
MRI shows fascial enhancement and fluid along fascial planes
Plain radiograph may show subcutaneous gas

differential.name: Abscess
differential.why_considered: A focal collection of pus in the skin and soft tissue can present with redness, warmth, tenderness, and fever, overlapping with cellulitis.

history: A focal, throbbing lump that is more localized than the diffuse spread of cellulitis
Often follows a boil, injection, or minor trauma
May have already been treated with oral antibiotics without improvement
exam: A fluctuant, dome-shaped, tender mass with a pointing center
Surrounding cellulitis may be present but the focal collection is palpable
Purulent drainage may be expressed
labs: WBC and CRP may be elevated but do not distinguish abscess from cellulitis
imaging: Ultrasound shows a well-defined fluid collection with posterior acoustic enhancement
CT shows a rim-enhancing fluid collection

differential.name: Stasis dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic venous insufficiency causes bilateral lower leg redness, swelling, and warmth that can be mistaken for cellulitis.

history: Long-standing leg swelling and varicose veins
Chronic, slowly progressive redness rather than acute onset over 1–3 days
No fever or chills
Itching and weeping rather than pain
exam: Bilateral, symmetric lower leg erythema and edema
Brown hemosiderin staining, varicose veins, and lipodermatosclerosis
No sharply warm, spreading plaque and no skin break at the edge
imaging: Venous duplex shows venous reflux or obstruction without soft tissue infection

differential.name: Contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Localized redness, swelling, and tenderness of the skin can resemble early cellulitis, especially on the hands or face.

history: Exposure to a new soap, plant, metal, or topical agent
Intense itching rather than pain
No fever or systemic symptoms
exam: Well-demarcated erythema with vesicles or weeping, often in a pattern matching the exposure
No warmth out of proportion and no lymphangitic streaking
No skin break or bite at the leading edge

differential.name: Gout
differential.why_considered: An acutely swollen, red, hot, and tender joint can be mistaken for cellulitis overlying a joint, especially at the first metatarsophalangeal joint or knee.

history: Sudden onset of severe joint pain reaching maximum intensity within hours
Prior similar attacks, alcohol use, or diuretic use
No skin break or bite
exam: Joint effusion, warmth, and extreme tenderness localized to the joint
Tophi may be present
No spreading erythema beyond the joint
labs: Elevated uric acid between attacks; may be normal during an attack
Joint aspiration shows needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals
imaging: Ultrasound shows a double contour sign or joint effusion
Plain radiograph may show erosions in chronic disease

differential.name: Septic arthritis
differential.why_considered: A hot, swollen, painful joint with fever can mimic cellulitis overlying a joint.
differential.trigger: Joint effusion with inability to bear weight or move the joint, especially with fever

history: Fever and chills with a single swollen joint
Recent joint surgery, injection, or bacteremia
Inability to bear weight
exam: Large joint effusion with markedly reduced range of motion
Tenderness localized to the joint line
No spreading skin erythema or skin break
labs: Joint aspiration shows purulent fluid with elevated WBC and positive Gram stain or culture
imaging: Plain radiograph may show joint space narrowing or erosions in late disease

differential.name: Hidradenitis suppurativa
differential.why_considered: Recurrent painful boils and draining sinus tracts in the axillae, groin, or under the breasts can be mistaken for recurrent cellulitis.

history: Recurrent boils and draining sinuses over months to years
Involvement of intertriginous areas such as axillae, groin, and inframammary folds
Family history of similar lesions
Often associated with obesity and smoking
exam: Comedones, double-ended pseudocomedones, nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts
Scarring and rope-like tracts in the affected areas
No spreading erythema beyond the affected follicles
labs: WBC and CRP may be elevated during flares but are not diagnostic
imaging: Ultrasound shows subcutaneous nodules, fluid collections, and sinus tracts

severity.mild: Uncomplicated cellulitis: limited area of erythema, no systemic symptoms, able to take oral antibiotics, no significant comorbidity.
severity.moderate: Cellulitis with fever, chills, or moderate pain; larger area of involvement; may need IV antibiotics or observation.
severity.severe: Cellulitis with systemic toxicity, rapid progression, or significant comorbidity; requires IV antibiotics and admission.
severity.critical: Cellulitis complicated by sepsis with hypotension, altered mental status, or organ dysfunction; or progression to necrotizing soft tissue infection.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests necrotizing soft tissue infection; needs urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Dusky, gray, or black skin; bullae with sloughing; or anesthesia over the area
red_flags.meaning: Suggests necrotizing soft tissue infection; needs urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Crepitus or crackling under the skin
red_flags.meaning: Suggests gas-forming infection or necrotizing soft tissue infection; needs urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia, or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Suggests sepsis; needs IV fluids, IV antibiotics, and admission

red_flags.finding: Rapid progression of erythema over hours
red_flags.meaning: Suggests aggressive infection or necrotizing soft tissue infection; reassess and consider surgical consultation

red_flags.finding: Failure to improve after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Consider abscess, resistant organism, or alternative diagnosis; reassess and image

complications.name: Abscess formation
clues: Fluctuant mass within the area of cellulitis

complications.name: Lymphangitis
clues: Red streak running proximally from the area of cellulitis

complications.name: Recurrent cellulitis
clues: Prior episodes at the same site
Persistent risk factors such as tinea pedis, lymphedema, or venous insufficiency

key_questions.question: When did the redness start, and has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset over 1–3 days with steady enlargement of the red area; rapid spread over hours raises concern for a necrotizing infection

key_questions.question: Where did it start, and did you notice a cut, scrape, bite, or crack in the skin there?
key_questions.looking_for: A portal of entry such as an insect bite, abrasion, surgical wound, or fissure between the toes

key_questions.question: How bad is the pain, and is it worse than the redness would suggest?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain proportionate to the visible inflammation; pain far out of proportion suggests necrotizing soft tissue infection

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and chills suggest systemic involvement and a need for IV antibiotics or admission

key_questions.question: Is the skin turning dark, gray, or black, or are there blisters or peeling?
key_questions.looking_for: Dusky or black skin, bullae with sloughing, or numbness — features of necrotizing soft tissue infection requiring urgent surgical evaluation

key_questions.question: Does the area crackle or pop when you press it, or do you feel gas under the skin?
key_questions.looking_for: Crepitus suggests a gas-forming or necrotizing infection

key_questions.question: Have you had this kind of infection before in the same spot?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior episodes at the same site suggest ongoing risk factors such as tinea pedis, lymphedema, or venous insufficiency

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, leg swelling, lymphedema, or a weakened immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that lower the threshold for admission and IV antibiotics and predict a worse course

key_questions.question: Are you taking prednisone, methotrexate, or a biologic such as infliximab or adalimumab?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression, which can blunt local signs and speed progression

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent long flight, surgery, or period of immobility, or any prior blood clot in the leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Features that raise the possibility of deep vein thrombosis as a competing diagnosis

key_questions.question: Do you inject drugs, or have you had a recent animal bite or fresh water exposure with an open wound?
key_questions.looking_for: Unusual exposures that broaden the organism differential and change antibiotic choice

key_questions.question: Any allergies to antibiotics, especially penicillins or cephalosporins?
Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status before antibiotics or imaging that could affect a pregnancy

key_questions.question: Any nausea, vomiting, or feeling generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic symptoms that support a more severe course

key_questions.question: Any numbness or loss of feeling over the red area?
key_questions.looking_for: Sensory loss over the involved skin suggests necrotizing soft tissue infection

reasoning_points: Acute onset over 1–3 days of a spreading, warm, tender, poorly demarcated red area, usually on the lower leg
A portal of entry such as an insect bite, abrasion, surgical wound, or interdigital fissure
Fever, chills, or malaise supporting a systemic bacterial infection
Risk factors such as diabetes, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, obesity, or immunosuppression
No fluctuance, crepitus, dusky skin, or pain out of proportion, which argues against abscess and necrotizing soft tissue infection
Alternative diagnoses such as deep vein thrombosis, stasis dermatitis, contact dermatitis, gout, or septic arthritis considered and excluded
Diagnosis is clinical; antibiotics should not be delayed for cultures or imaging in uncomplicated cases
Pregnancy excluded before antibiotics or imaging when applicable

easy: Classic lower leg presentation with a clear insect bite or abrasion
Fever and chills with a warm, spreading red plaque
medium: Older adult with diabetes and a foot ulcer, less striking redness and blunted pain
Bilateral leg swelling from venous insufficiency making the asymmetry harder to see
Mild pyuria or nonspecific labs that raise a urinary or other source
Patient with prior cellulitis at the same site and ongoing tinea pedis
hard: Immunocompromised patient with fever but minimal local signs
Pain out of proportion with early dusky skin suggesting necrotizing soft tissue infection
Pregnant patient with leg swelling mistaken for normal pregnancy changes
Failure to improve after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics suggesting an occult abscess or resistant organism
Injection drug user with an atypical organism or a deep collection
